strengths: Introduces a genuinely new and useful resource: SwissGov-RSD is the first human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level semantic difference recognition, addressing an under-studied but practically important task (RSD) with naturalistic, real-world parallel government documents.

Comprehensive and well-structured evaluation: the paper benchmarks unsupervised (DiffAlign), few-shot prompted LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, and fine-tuned encoder models across three language pairs and two datasets (synthetic iSTS-RSD vs. natural SwissGov-RSD), including qualitative error analysis, position-in-document analysis, and inference-time comparisons.

Strong reproducibility: code and dataset are released, annotation guidelines are provided in full (Appendix A.2), the annotation interface and process are documented in detail, and the data collection pipeline (scraping, filtering, labeling scheme, validation) is transparently described.

The central finding that synthetically augmented data (iSTS-RSD) does not transfer to naturalistic cross-lingual document-level RSD, with substantial drops in Spearman correlation, is well supported by the evidence and is a valuable cautionary result for the community.

The paper is clearly written, with helpful figures (label distribution, architecture diagrams, annotation strategy disagreements) and appropriate attention to limitations (language/script diversity, annotation consistency, prompting limitations).

Careful reporting of annotation statistics and inter-annotator agreement, including a trial phase, targeted feedback, and a comparison to prior work (Kocmi et al., 2024) showing the reported agreement is within normal ranges.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is relatively low (mean IoU 10-43%, mean F1 17-56%), which raises concerns about the reliability of the gold labels and the stability of system rankings on this benchmark; the authors acknowledge this but it materially limits confidence in the benchmark.

The dataset is modest in size (224 document pairs per language pair, ~173k-187k tokens), and the two-annotator setup with overlap on only 25 documents per language pair restricts the strength of the validation; the claim that agreement 'improves' after feedback is based on a small sample.

The language scope is narrow: all pairs are English-centric and limited to high-resource, closely related Latin-script languages (German, French, Italian). This constrains the generalizability of the benchmark and the conclusions drawn from it, which the authors themselves note.

The paper is primarily a dataset/benchmark contribution with limited methodological novelty; the automatic approaches evaluated are largely existing methods, and the analysis does not propose new modeling solutions to the identified gap.

Some comparisons may not be fully controlled: fine-tuning budgets differ across models (e.g., 560 augmentations for LLMs vs. 10,000 for encoders), and resource constraints lead to inconsistent evaluation coverage across settings, which complicates interpretation of relative model performance.

The very low absolute correlations on SwissGov-RSD (e.g., near-zero or negative for several systems) make it difficult to distinguish genuine model failure from a task/metric that may be poorly specified or extremely hard, and the paper does not deeply interrogate whether Spearman correlation over heavily skewed, tie-heavy labels is the most appropriate metric.

strengths: Introduces the first human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level semantic difference recognition (RSD), covering English–German, English–French, and English–Italian. This addresses a clear gap left by synthetic iSTS-RSD and provides a much-needed naturalistic benchmark.

The dataset is constructed from naturally occurring Swiss government documents, with detailed annotation guidelines, a trial phase, overlap-based quality checks, and released labels/code (with copyright notices). The annotation interface and process are documented in appendices, aiding reproducibility.

The benchmark is broad and thorough: unsupervised DiffAlign, few-shot prompting with several LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, and multiple encoder models (XLM-R, LaBSE, ModernBERT, EuroBERT, etc.) are compared on both iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD, with additional Kendall τ, output-failure, position-in-document, and annotation-discrepancy analyses.

The central empirical claim is well supported: models that perform strongly on synthetic iSTS-RSD drop dramatically on SwissGov-RSD (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini falls from 78–82 Spearman to near zero), convincingly showing that synthetic augmentation alone does not prepare systems for realistic cross-lingual document-level RSD.
The paper is clearly written, well structured, and candid about limitations, including language diversity, annotation consistency, and prompting simplicity.
weaknesses: Annotation reliability is limited. Only 25 overlapping documents per language pair are used for agreement, most annotations are from a single annotator, and the final merge manually selects annotations that adhere to guidelines rather than using full adjudication. Reported span agreement is low (mean IoU 10–32, mean F1 17–55), which may make gold labels noisy and system rankings unstable.

The dataset is modest in scale and scope: 224 multi-parallel document sets (886 texts) across only three high-resource European language pairs, with no standard train/dev/test split. This limits the benchmark’s utility for future supervised work and somewhat weakens reproducibility as a shared evaluation resource.

The main metric—token-level Spearman/Kendall correlation over heavily skewed labels (only ~10–17% of tokens are non-zero)—can be sensitive to tie handling and class imbalance. The paper lacks random/majority baselines, significance tests for model comparisons, and confidence intervals, making some model ranking claims fragile.

No in-domain supervised baseline is provided: no model is trained on SwissGov-RSD data. The conclusion that “all systems perform poorly” therefore applies only to zero-shot, few-shot, or synthetic-trained settings, which may overstate the intrinsic difficulty of the task and leaves open how much in-domain training would help.

Some methodological choices are not fully justified or specified: splitting long documents for 512-token encoders such as DiffAlign is not described in detail; few-shot prompts are intentionally simple; heuristics for parsing malformed LLM outputs could affect scores; and cross-lingual label projection with GPT-4o-mini is validated only on a small sample.

Reproducibility is partially constrained by reliance on proprietary API models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o3-mini) that can change over time, and by copyright restrictions on the source text, which may hinder full data redistribution despite the labels being released.

strengths: Introduces SwissGov-RSD, a new human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual benchmark for token-level semantic difference recognition, addressing an underexplored and practically relevant NLP task.

Provides detailed annotation guidelines, an interactive annotation interface, and a validation procedure with a trial phase and overlapping annotations, and releases labels/code under an open license.
Benchmarks a broad set of systems—unsupervised DiffAlign, few-shot and fine-tuned LLMs, and encoder models—on both SwissGov-RSD and iSTS-RSD, enabling useful comparisons.
Reports informative analyses of failure modes, including LLM formatting failures, length sensitivity, label distributions, and inference time.

Shows a clear and useful negative result: models tuned on synthetic/augmented iSTS-RSD transfer poorly to naturalistic cross-lingual documents, while unsupervised encoder-based methods are relatively robust.
weaknesses: Annotation quality and benchmark reliability are major concerns: inter-annotator agreement is low, especially for EN-DE (e.g., mean IoU around 11 and F1 around 18; large discrepancies in number of annotated differences), only 25 overlapping documents are used, and the final merge process is described vaguely as including annotations that adhere more to guidelines and label distribution, making the gold labels subjective and not fully reproducible.

There are no train/dev/test splits for SwissGov-RSD; all 224 documents are used for evaluation, so the benchmark does not support in-domain training or fine-tuning, and the reported poor performance is only zero-shot transfer rather than a fair estimate of achievable in-domain performance.

Methodological inconsistencies undermine reproducibility: fine-tuned encoder training is described as minimizing binary cross-entropy for continuous regression targets, and the label projection prompt in Appendix D uses a similarity scale (5 = complete equivalence) while the main paper defines difference labels (5 = complete dissimilarity), raising concerns about label orientation and training data correctness.

Evaluation is limited to token-level Spearman/Kendall correlations; despite span-level annotations, no span-level precision/recall/F1 is reported, and the highly imbalanced label distribution (only 10–17% difference labels) means the reported correlations may not reflect practical RSD performance.

The claims are somewhat overbroad: only three high-resource, English-centric European language pairs are covered, Romansh is excluded, related comparable corpora exist, and the paper does not fully isolate the effect of domain/label-distribution shift from synthetic-vs-naturalistic differences.

Experimental reporting is inconsistent and confusing: main Table 3 and Appendix Table 11 give very different iSTS-RSD numbers, LLM evaluation subsets are restricted for computational reasons, and it is unclear which results are directly comparable.
No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are provided for model comparisons, so small differences among systems may not be meaningful.

The dataset is relatively small (224 documents per language pair), and the annotation setup (two annotators per language pair, 20–35 hours each) raises concerns about depth and consistency, especially for complex omission/addition cases.

strengths: The paper introduces SwissGov-RSD, a new human-annotated, multi-parallel, document-level benchmark for token-level cross-lingual semantic difference recognition, covering English-German, English-French, and English-Italian.

The task is practically relevant and underexplored: detecting naturally occurring semantic differences in multilingual government documents, where omissions or updates can cause meaning mismatches across language versions.

The dataset construction is described in substantial detail, including crawling and filtering, annotation guidelines, trial phase, overlap-based validation, compensation, and release/licensing information.
The evaluation is broad, comparing unsupervised DiffAlign, encoder models, few-shot LLMs, and fine-tuned LLMs/encoders across synthetic iSTS-RSD and the new realistic benchmark.
The central empirical finding—that systems performing well on synthetic iSTS-RSD degrade substantially on SwissGov-RSD—is supported and useful for motivating future realistic cross-lingual RSD work.
The paper reports model failure modes such as LLM output formatting errors, long-document degradation, and low performance on the realistic benchmark, which are valuable diagnostic insights.
Limitations are acknowledged, including language coverage, annotation consistency, and prompting simplicity.
weaknesses: Annotation reliability is only moderate: inter-annotator token-level Spearman correlations range from about 43.6 to 65.1, with only 25 overlapping documents and two annotators per language pair; there is no final inter-annotator agreement reported for the full dataset.

The paper does not clearly reconcile the reversed SwissGov-RSD difference scale with the iSTS-style similarity prompts used for few-shot LLM evaluation and label projection. As written, it is ambiguous how similarity/difference scores were mapped before training and correlation computation, which affects reproducibility and interpretation.

Evaluation relies almost exclusively on token-level Spearman/Kendall correlations. There is no human upper bound, no breakdown by difference type (omission, addition, substitution), and no significance testing or confidence intervals.

The comparison between iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD is not fully balanced: iSTS-RSD evaluation is restricted to 100 samples per difficulty setting, while SwissGov-RSD is evaluated on the full dataset; LLM fine-tuning also uses far fewer augmentations than encoder fine-tuning, potentially confounding dataset effects with training-scale differences.

The dataset covers only high-resource, closely related, Latin-script, English-centric language pairs. This limits claims about generalizability to typologically diverse or non-Latin-script languages, as the authors acknowledge.

The label projection procedure using GPT-4o-mini is only evaluated on 50 samples per language pair; residual projection errors may affect the fine-tuned cross-lingual encoder results, and the effect is not quantified on downstream performance.

The claim that this is the first naturalistic document-level cross-lingual dataset for token-level RSD could be better justified against related corpora such as SwissAdmin and 20min-XD; the distinction is plausible but not fully established.

The paper's conclusion that current systems struggle on realistic RSD is supported, but the extremely low SwissGov-RSD scores may partly reflect metric sensitivity, label distribution (only 10–17% of tokens labeled different), and domain/length shift rather than purely task difficulty.

strengths: Introduces SwissGov-RSD, a novel human-annotated document-level cross-lingual benchmark for token-level RSD in EN-DE/FR/IT, addressing a clear gap between synthetic iSTS-RSD and real-world administrative texts.

Annotation methodology is relatively thorough: pilot/trial phase, written guidelines, two annotators per language pair, overlap validation, compensation, manual quality checks, and transparent reporting of limitations.

Broad evaluation spanning unsupervised alignment, few-shot LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, and encoder models; reveals substantial performance drop from iSTS-RSD to SwissGov-RSD and practical LLM issues such as format failures and long-context degradation.
Reproducibility is supported by released code/labels, prompts, model/hyperparameter details, annotation interface, and extensive appendices; suitable for Findings-level reproducibility.
Useful negative results: fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini overfits synthetic augmentations; unsupervised DiffAlign/encoders remain competitive on realistic data, suggesting directions for future work.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is modest (224 multi-parallel documents, ~173k-195k tokens per language pair) and restricted to high-resource, English-centric European languages; broader typological/script diversity remains untested.

Annotation agreement is only moderate (token-level Spearman 43.6-65.1; IoU 24-43; F1 33-56), with only 25 overlapping documents for validation and a manual merge of annotations, raising label-noise and potential bias concerns.

The main metric (token-level Spearman over all tokens, with unannotated tokens assumed equivalent) is sensitive to skewed label distribution and annotation noise; Kendall results are low, and evaluation does not fully separate model error from annotation uncertainty.

Some methodological details are unclear or inconsistent: encoder training is described as minimizing binary cross-entropy on continuous 0-1 scores while SwissGov labels are 0-5; normalization and exact loss are not specified, affecting reproducibility and baseline strength.

The claim that synthetic benchmarks 'do not sufficiently reflect' realistic scenarios is supported by one synthetic benchmark (iSTS-RSD) and one real dataset; related real-world corpora are discussed but not benchmarked, limiting generality.

Due to computational constraints, not all systems are evaluated on SwissGov-RSD, and system selection is based on iSTS-RSD performance; this may bias comparisons, especially for LLMs. Dataset redistribution is label-only, so full text reproducibility depends on crawling a changing website.

strengths: Introduces a new human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual benchmark for token-level semantic difference recognition, addressing an under-explored and practically relevant task.
Dataset construction is well documented, including annotation guidelines, interface details, trial phase, annotator compensation, and licensing/release plans.
Evaluates a wide range of systems (unsupervised, few-shot LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, encoder models) across English–German, English–French, and English–Italian, and compares with iSTS-RSD.
Provides a useful negative result: model performance drops substantially from synthetic iSTS-RSD to naturalistic SwissGov-RSD, suggesting synthetic benchmarks may overestimate real-world RSD ability.
The limitations section candidly acknowledges language/script coverage, annotation consistency, and prompting limitations.
Code and data are promised publicly, with annotation scripts and guidelines included, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that synthetic benchmarks fail to reflect realistic scenarios is confounded: fine-tuned models are evaluated in-domain on iSTS-RSD but zero-shot on SwissGov-RSD, while domain shift, document length, annotation scheme, and label distribution also differ. The comparison therefore does not isolate syntheticness as the cause.

Annotation reliability is low (Spearman 43.6–65.1), and the paper reports replacing one EN-DE annotator after poor initial agreement. This raises serious concerns about gold-label quality and the benchmark's validity for fine-grained token-level evaluation.

Several model results are missing on SwissGov-RSD (e.g., fine-tuned Llama-3.1 8B, many encoder variants) due to computational constraints, and iSTS-RSD evaluation uses only 100 samples per setting, weakening statistical robustness.

The evaluation uses token-level Spearman correlation on span-level annotations but does not report model span-level F1/IoU or a human upper bound beyond inter-annotator agreement, limiting insight into actual semantic difference recognition performance.
Label projection for training encoder models uses GPT-4o-mini and requires edits in 34–46% of samples, but the impact of this noise on model results is not fully analyzed.

Scale reporting is inconsistent: Table 3 values appear to be multiplied by 100 while Table 7 uses decimals, and Figure 5 shows y-axis values above 1 without explanation. Handling of reversed label scales between iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD is also unclear.

Unsupervised DiffAlign results on SwissGov-RSD require input splitting due to length limits, making comparisons with long-context systems unfair; the paper acknowledges this but still draws strong conclusions from the gap.
There are no training/validation/test splits for SwissGov-RSD and no in-domain training baseline, so it remains unclear whether current models could learn the task with naturalistic supervision.

LLM failures are partly caused by output formatting and sequence-length mismatches (Table 4), but the paper does not fully disentangle these engineering issues from genuine semantic-understanding failures.
Broad claims about monolingual and sentence-level benchmarks are not directly tested; the experimental comparison is limited to iSTS-RSD.
